title: Rapid fire and the final checklist
brief: Twenty-four questions, one or more per chapter, then the ten questions to ask about any AI system you have never seen and the five-step method that turns the answers into a defended design. Run the quiz against a timer, then keep the table as your map.

blocks.text: How to run the rapid fire

blocks.md: Give each question about 90 seconds and say the dial that decides it out loud before you pick. The set covers every chapter from the orientation to the field notes, in all five question types. A miss is a pointer: the explanation names the mechanism, and the table below tells you which topic to reopen.

blocks.text: Ten questions to ask about any unfamiliar AI system

blocks.caption: Ask these in order. Each answer lives in the topics listed in the last column.
head: Question
Why it decides the design
Where the answer lives
rows: What is it for, and which actions can it take?
Autonomy and reversibility set the pattern and the oversight level.
Where does knowledge come from, how does it get in and how does it stay current?
Parsing quality, change detection and deletes cap everything downstream.
Who may see what, and what enforces it at query time?
The model can only leak what retrieval hands it.
How is content split, embedded and indexed?
Chunk, embedding and filter choices set the recall ceiling.
How does retrieval find the right chunk for exact identifiers and for paraphrases?
Lexical, dense, hybrid and rerank each fail on a different query type.
Which guards stand where, and what does a false alarm cost?
Guards add latency and refusals, and they check content, not permissions.
How are state, context and tool access managed?
API choice, token scoping and context budgets decide portability and blast radius.
What does one answer cost, how long does it take and what breaks at a 429 or an outage?
Latency budgets and capacity modes set the user experience under load.
How do you know it works, and how would you know why it failed?
Evidence before launch and traces after it keep a wrong answer explainable.
Who is accountable, where does it run and which rules apply?
Identity, residency and law decide what may ship at all.

blocks.title: Dial and Defend in five minutes

steps.title: Clarify the dials
steps.md: Corpus, update rate, permission model, tenancy, latency, risk and cost.

steps.title: List the options
steps.md: At least two, including the boring one, each with where it loses.

steps.title: Pick and flip
steps.md: Choose for the stated dials and name the change that reverses the choice.

steps.title: Name the failures
steps.md: Symptom, cause and the signal that detects it.

steps.title: Metrics and rollout
steps.md: Golden set, SLOs, shadow, canary and a kill switch.

blocks.title: The habit that separates strong answers
blocks.md: Never end on the pick. End on what would change your mind and how you would find out you were wrong. An answer with a flip condition and a detection signal reads as experience, not recall.

quiz.q: Put the five steps of the Dial-and-Defend method in order.
items: Clarify the dials: corpus, update rate, permission model, tenancy, latency, risk and cost
List the options, including the boring one
Pick for the stated dials and say what would flip the choice
Name the failure modes and how you would detect them
Name the metrics and the rollout plan
quiz.explain: Clarifying comes first because the dials decide which options are even valid. Options come before the pick so the choice is visible as a trade-off. Failure modes and detection come after the pick, because they belong to the chosen design, and metrics and rollout close the answer with how you would prove it works.

quiz.q: Replies from the second call ignore the house style set in the system prompt. What is the bug?

code.code:
r1 = client.responses.create(model=MODEL, instructions=SYSTEM, input="Summarize ticket 41")
r2 = client.responses.create(model=MODEL, previous_response_id=r1.id, input="Draft a reply")

options: `instructions` are not carried over by `previous_response_id`, so send them again on the second call
`previous_response_id` works only when `store` is set to false on the first call, so the chain never forms
Chained responses accept only a single hop, so the second call loses everything from the first one
`previous_response_id` cannot be combined with `input`, so the new text overwrites the whole chain
quiz.explain: With `previous_response_id`, top-level `instructions` do not carry over, so the second call runs without the system prompt. Responses are stored by default for 30 days, which is what makes chaining work, and the earlier input tokens are billed again on each call. The other options describe limits that do not exist: `store` false would break chaining, chains are not limited to one hop, and `input` is the way to add the new turn.

quiz.q: On GPT-5.6 and later models other than GPT-6.1 Sol a cache write costs 1.25 times and a read 0.1 times the uncached input rate. A shared prefix is written once and read 19 more times within the TTL. What is the total prefix cost as a multiple of reading it once at the uncached rate?
quiz.explain: 1.25 + 19 x 0.1 = 3.15, against 20 for twenty uncached reads, about 84 percent less. The same arithmetic shows the risk: a prefix written and never reused costs 1.25, a 25 percent premium, so cache only prefixes that repeat within the TTL.

quiz.q: Users still get answers that cite blobs deleted from storage last week. The blob indexer runs hourly and reports success. What is the cause?
options: The hourly schedule is below the minimum indexer interval, so every other run is silently skipped by the service
A delete updates LastModified on the blob, so the indexer re-indexes the deleted file with its old content
It tracks changes by LastModified and does not detect deletes without a deletion policy such as soft delete
The semantic ranker keeps the last 50 results cached and serves them even after the source blob is deleted
quiz.explain: The blob indexer finds changes through LastModified and does not see deletions unless a deletion detection policy, such as soft delete, is configured. A restored soft-deleted blob is not re-indexed either, because LastModified does not change. The minimum schedule interval is 5 minutes, so hourly is valid, a delete is not a LastModified change, and the semantic ranker works on the live result set rather than a cache.

quiz.q: An index holds 10 million vectors of 1,536 dimensions stored as float32. Ignoring HNSW overhead, how many GB do the raw vectors need after scalar (int8) quantization?
quiz.hint: float32 uses 4 bytes per dimension, int8 uses 1.
quiz.explain: 10,000,000 x 1,536 = 15.36 billion values. At float32 that is 61.44 GB and at int8, 4 times smaller, it is 15.36 GB. In Azure AI Search the vector index quota is a memory quota and HNSW adds 1 to 20 percent on top. Binary quantization goes further, up to about 28 times smaller and best above 1,024 dimensions, and rescoring with oversampling recovers recall.

quiz.q: For an exact question the right document sits at rank 120 of the first-stage results. Enabling the semantic ranker does not surface it. Why?
options: The semantic ranker summarizes at most 2,048 tokens per document, so long documents always score low
It reranks only the top 50 results of BM25 or RRF and cannot rerun the query to find new documents
Semantic ranking needs an `orderBy` clause to place the best document first in the result list
Semantic ranking works only on `search=*`, which skips first-stage scoring for the whole query
quiz.explain: A reranker reorders a candidate list and cannot add to it, so a document outside the top 50 never reaches it. Fix recall in the first stage: hybrid retrieval, better chunks, a larger candidate set (k plus maxTextRecallSize at least 50) and metadata filters. An `orderBy` clause returns HTTP 400 with semantic ranking, an empty or `*` query cannot be semantically ranked, and the 2,048-token cap limits what is read per document, not which documents are considered.

quiz.q: An assistant streams answers, and compliance says no unfiltered text may ever reach the screen. Which content filter streaming mode do you choose?
options: Asynchronous filter mode, because tokens stream at once and the filter signal always arrives before the text is shown
Asynchronous filter mode, because its filtering signal is guaranteed over the whole length of every answer
Filtering off while streaming, with a nightly review of saved transcripts to catch any problems later
Default streaming, which buffers text, filters it and returns it in chunks at the cost of some delay
quiz.explain: In default streaming the text is buffered, filtered and then returned in chunks, so nothing unfiltered is shown, at a latency cost. In asynchronous filter mode the signal is guaranteed only within a roughly 1,000-character window, so text can be shown before it is judged. Flip to asynchronous mode only when perceived latency matters more and a late retraction is acceptable, for example low-risk content with post-hoc redaction.

quiz.q: Which statements about native document-level ACL queries in Azure AI Search (preview as of 2026-10-13) are correct? Choose all that apply.
options: The caller's Entra token goes in the `x-ms-query-source-authorization` header
From 2025-11-01-preview an API key or admin role bypasses the ACL filter
A request with no user token returns only public documents
If group resolution through Microsoft Graph fails, the query returns partial results
Permission fields use Entra object ids, not user principal names
quiz.explain: The user's token travels in the query-source header, a missing token returns only public documents from 2025-11-01-preview, and permission fields hold object ids. Since that version the ACL filter applies even with an API key or an admin role, so the bypass statement is wrong, and a Graph failure returns a 5xx error rather than a partial result, which is the safe default.

quiz.q: An MCP server receives an access token from the client and forwards it unchanged to a downstream API to save a token exchange. What is wrong?
options: Token passthrough, which the specification forbids: a server must accept only tokens issued for it
Nothing is wrong, as long as the token's scopes already cover the downstream API it is forwarded to
The token must first be wrapped in an `Mcp-Session-Id` header before it can be forwarded downstream
The token is too short-lived, so the server should cache it and reuse it across users and sessions
quiz.explain: MCP servers must not accept tokens that were not issued for them, and passing a client's token downstream makes the server a confused deputy. Clients send the RFC 8707 resource parameter so tokens are audience-bound, and the server obtains its own downstream token, for example by an on-behalf-of exchange. Matching scopes do not fix a wrong audience, the session header is unrelated, and sharing a cached token across users is a leak.

quiz.q: A client sends a refinement to a task in the COMPLETED state, using that task's id, and the server rejects it. What is the right continuation?
options: Task ids are client-generated, so the id collided: generate a new UUID and resend to the same task
The server lacks the push notification capability: enable it on the Agent Card and resend the message
A terminal task cannot restart, so send the refinement as a new task in the same contextId
COMPLETED is an interrupted state: call SubscribeToTask first to resume the task before sending
quiz.explain: COMPLETED, FAILED, CANCELED and REJECTED are terminal, so refinements start a new task in the same contextId and may point back with referenceTaskIds. INPUT_REQUIRED and AUTH_REQUIRED are the interrupted states, where a message continues the same task. Task ids are server-generated, and push notifications concern delivery of updates, not whether a task can restart.

quiz.q: Which change in the workload most justifies moving from one agent to parallel subagents?
options: The subtasks begin writing to the same files and must agree on a number of shared decisions
The work becomes read-heavy research over independent sources, worth several times the tokens
The prompt grows by ten sentences of style rules that the model sometimes follows and sometimes ignores
The latency target tightens, but each step needs the previous step's output
quiz.explain: Independent reads parallelize, and Anthropic reports parallel subagents cutting research time by up to 90 percent while multi-agent systems use about 15 times the tokens of chat, so the value per task must justify the cost. Parallel writers that share decisions conflict, which is Cognition's argument against them. Style rules are a prompt fix, and sequential dependencies cannot run in parallel. Start at the lowest level of complexity that meets the need.

quiz.q: After a deployment, resuming from last week's workflow checkpoint fails. The new build renamed several executors and rewired two edges. What explains it?
options: Checkpoints store only the final output, so an intermediate step can never be resumed from them
Checkpoints are written once before the first superstep, so later steps are always recomputed from scratch
File checkpoint storage cannot be read by a newer build of the same package, whatever else changed
A checkpoint is tied to the workflow's topology and executor ids, so renaming or rewiring breaks resume
quiz.explain: A checkpoint is created at the end of each superstep and holds executor state, pending messages, pending requests and responses and shared state, so it can only be restored into a workflow with the same topology and executor identities (in .NET, agents also need a stable Id and an unchanged Name). Version workflows deliberately and drain or migrate old runs. The first two options misstate what is stored and when, and storage format is not the issue.

quiz.q: You want to canary a new hosted agent version on 5 percent of traffic. What works?
options: Deploy the version as a second agent and split traffic in the client or a gateway
Set a 5 percent traffic weight between two versions on the same agent endpoint, since it routes by weight
Add a second sandbox size to the same version so that a share of sessions receives the new build
Create two sessions per user and let the platform alternate between versions as requests arrive
quiz.explain: A hosted agent endpoint serves one version with 100 percent of traffic and traffic splitting is not supported, so a canary is a second agent with the split done by the caller or a gateway. Compare evaluation and trace metrics, then promote. Sandbox sizes belong to a version, and sessions do not alternate between versions.

quiz.q: A voice agent keeps cutting in when a user pauses mid-sentence. It uses `server_vad`. What do you try first?
options: Raise the output sampling rate so replies start faster than the pause the user takes
Switch to a larger model, because turn endings depend on how deeply the model reasons
Use `semantic_vad` with low eagerness, so end of turn depends on meaning, not only silence
Turn detection off, and commit the audio buffer manually every 100 ms of incoming audio
quiz.explain: `server_vad` is silence-based, so a thinking pause looks like the end of a turn. `semantic_vad` with eagerness low waits longer for a finished thought, and in noisy settings the silence threshold and duration can also be tuned. Sampling rate and model size do not change turn detection, and committing the buffer manually is the pattern for transcription-only models, not a fix for interruptions.

quiz.q: Four queries have their first relevant result at ranks 1, 3, none and 2. What is the mean reciprocal rank (MRR)?
quiz.hint: A query with no relevant result contributes 0.
quiz.explain: The reciprocal ranks are 1, 0.333, 0 and 0.5, which sum to 1.833, and dividing by 4 gives 0.458. MRR rewards getting one relevant result high and ignores everything after it, so pair it with recall at k when the answer needs several chunks.

quiz.q: Spans from an Agent Framework agent and from the MCP server it calls show up as separate traces. The tool is a provider-managed MCP tool. Why?
options: MCP forbids trace context in messages, so joining the two traces is impossible by design of the protocol
It injects `traceparent` into `params._meta` only for MCP sessions it opens, not provider-managed tools
A 5 percent sampling ratio always drops the child spans of tool calls, so they never join the parent
The server needs the trace id in the `Mcp-Session-Id` header before it can join the existing trace
quiz.explain: MCP carries W3C trace context as `traceparent`, `tracestate` and `baggage` in `params._meta`, and the 2026-07-28 revision reserves those keys. Agent Framework Python injects them only for sessions it opens (MCPStreamableHTTPTool, MCPStdioTool, MCPWebsocketTool), so a provider-managed tool never receives the context. Use a framework-opened MCP tool or propagate at a gateway. Sampling drops whole traces, not individual children, and the session header is unrelated.

quiz.q: A deployment has 90,000 TPM. Each request has 700 prompt tokens and sets max_tokens to 2,300, and the TPM check counts prompt plus max_tokens up front. At most how many requests per minute pass the check?
quiz.hint: Divide the quota by tokens counted per request.
quiz.explain: Each request counts 700 + 2,300 = 3,000 tokens against the limit, so 90,000 / 3,000 = 30 requests per minute. Setting max_tokens near the real answer length, say 500, counts 1,200 per request and admits 75. This is why a 429 can appear below the quota you think you are using.

quiz.q: Match each date to what the EU AI Act timeline puts there.

pairs.r: Article 50 transparency rules apply and enforcement starts
Annex III high-risk rules apply, as moved by the AI Omnibus

quiz.explain: These dates anchor a compliance conversation. Prohibitions and AI literacy came first, general-purpose AI obligations followed on 2025-08-02, Article 50 transparency applies from 2026-08-02 and the Omnibus moved Annex III high-risk rules to 2027-12-02, with Annex I rules on 2028-08-02. Verify against the current official timeline before relying on a date.

quiz.q: A reasoning-model call returns status `incomplete` with no visible text, and `max_output_tokens` is 800. What is the cause and the fix?
options: The model refused silently, so add a refusal handler to the client and surface the refusal text
The content filter blocked the answer, so lower the severity threshold for that content category
Streaming was off, so visible text was dropped by the client; turn streaming on to receive it
Reasoning tokens used the output budget before any visible text, so reserve 25,000 tokens at first
quiz.explain: Reasoning tokens bill as output and share the context window, so a small `max_output_tokens` can be spent before any visible text, which returns `incomplete`. OpenAI and Azure advise reserving at least 25,000 tokens when starting out, then tuning reasoning effort. Refusals and content filters produce different statuses, and streaming changes delivery, not the budget.

quiz.q: An agent reads customer emails (untrusted input), searches internal HR files (sensitive access) and can send external email. Which design follows the Agents Rule of Two?
options: Keep all three properties and add a stronger system prompt that forbids leaking HR data
Keep all three properties and log every external send for audit after the fact
Remove one of the three, or require human approval before the external send happens
Keep all three properties and run the model at temperature 0 so behavior is deterministic
quiz.explain: The Rule of Two says a session should hold no more than two of untrusted input, sensitive access and the ability to change state or communicate externally, and should require human approval or an equivalent when all three are needed. Prompts are not controls, audit after the fact does not prevent exfiltration and temperature 0 does not make injected instructions safe.

quiz.q: A static 60,000-token policy handbook is queried 40 times a minute by one assistant. Which design is the most defensible first choice?
options: Fine-tune a model on the handbook, because the content is static and rarely changes
Cache the handbook as a stable prefix and compare it with RAG on a golden set first
Always build a vector index first, because long prompts are never accurate enough for policy text
Send the handbook uncached on every call, because the cache write premium costs more than it saves
quiz.explain: A corpus under roughly 200,000 tokens can go in the prompt, and with 40 queries a minute the prefix is reused many times inside the TTL, so one write at 1.25 times and cheap reads at 0.1 times beat resending it. Long-context accuracy can still fall well before the advertised window (in NoLiMa, 11 of 13 models that claim 128K or more dropped below 50 percent of their short-context baseline at 32K [[r87]]), so measure against RAG. Flip to RAG when the corpus outgrows the window, changes often enough to bust the cache, needs per-user access control or needs passage-level citations.

quiz.q: Order a secure RAG request from first step to last.
items: Authenticate the user and resolve their groups
Screen the input, then retrieve with the permission filter applied
Generate the answer with citations from the allowed chunks
Check groundedness and constrain the rendered output
Emit trace spans and a retrieval log without raw content
quiz.explain: Identity comes first because the filter needs it. Retrieval must apply the permission filter before any reranking or generation, so the model never sees forbidden chunks. Output checks run on the finished answer, and telemetry closes the request with references rather than raw text.

quiz.q: Which practices make an LLM-as-judge setup more reliable? Choose all that apply.
options: Run pairwise comparisons in both orders and count only consistent verdicts
Give the judge a reference answer for math or factual grading
Use the same model that wrote the answer as the judge, to keep style consistent
Calibrate the judge against a human-labelled sample and track agreement
Prefer the longest answer when scores tie, because it is usually more complete
quiz.explain: Swapping order cancels position bias, a reference answer cut math grading failures from 14 of 20 to 3 of 20 in MT-Bench [[r73]], and a human-labelled calibration set shows whether the judge can be trusted at all. A judge that grades its own model's output tends to favor it, and preferring length rewards verbosity rather than correctness.

quiz.q: Match each MCP primitive or hint to who controls it or how it is treated.

pairs.r: Untrusted unless they come from a trusted server

quiz.explain: Tools are invoked by the model, resources are attached by the application and prompts are chosen by the user. Annotations such as readOnlyHint are hints, and clients must consider them untrusted unless the server is trusted, so never base a security decision on them alone.

takeaways: Ask the ten questions in order, because each one narrows which options are valid
Name the dial before you name the product, every time
Know the mechanisms behind the numbers: cache pricing, quotas, patch tokens, checkpoints and ACL behavior
End every answer with what would flip the choice and the signal that tells you it did
Date-stamp previews and retirements, because the freshness of a claim is part of the claim
